questions.explain: Serverless bills allocated (not used) vCores per vCore-second while active, storage per GB-month continuously — even while paused — and $0 compute once auto-pause engages. The minimum vCore setting is therefore a billing floor on every active second and trailing idle hour.
options: Compute only when queries run, nothing else
A flat monthly fee per database plus storage
Compute per vCore-second at the allocated vCore count, storage per GB-month continuously (even while paused), and zero compute while paused
Per-query billing based on rows scanned
questions.q: What are the three billing components of Azure SQL Database serverless?

questions.explain: Auto-pause delay (default 60 min, 1 hour to 7 days) is the most misunderstood parameter: every wake-up costs at minimum the delay window at the minimum vCore count. With 0.5 vCores and a 1-hour delay, each session costs at least 1,800 vCore-seconds before any query work.
options: Every wake-up costs at minimum the auto-pause delay window at the minimum vCore count — e.g., 1,800 vCore-seconds at 0.5 vCores with a 1-hour delay
Auto-pause resets billing to zero retroactively for the prior hour
The delay is charged only once per month
Auto-pause has no cost impact; it is purely a performance setting
questions.q: Why is the auto-pause delay the single most misunderstood serverless parameter?

questions.explain: Serverless wins on intermittent usage with multi-hour idle gaps (dev/QA nights and weekends, demos, batch targets, feature-branch databases). The diagnostic rule: idle (>95% below 5% CPU) less than 40% of the month → serverless likely costs more; more than 70% idle → usually a clear win; between 40–70%, run the worked math.
options: Databases with steady 24/7 utilization
Only databases under 10 GB
Any database previously on provisioned
Single databases with long idle gaps and unpredictable active periods; under 40% idle time serverless usually loses, over 70% idle it usually wins
questions.q: Which workload shape wins on serverless, and what is the chapter's 40/70 rule?

questions.explain: The fix: set minimum to 0.5 vCores unless measured latency evidence justifies more — the minimum is a billing floor, not a performance setting, since the database still auto-scales to the max. Audit monthly with the Resource Graph query; lowering the minimum needs no downtime.
options: Raise the minimum to 16 vCores for safety margin
Set the minimum to 0.5 vCores unless measured latency data justifies more — it is a billing floor, not a performance setting
Match the minimum to the old provisioned size to be safe
Disable auto-scaling and keep the maximum at 40 vCores
questions.q: What causes the vCore floor problem, and what is the fix?

questions.explain: The usual keep-awake suspects: uptime/synthetic monitors (a 5-minute ping means the database never reaches the 60-minute idle threshold), aggressive connection-pool validation queries, hourly jobs, and developer tooling left open. The switch-back rule: migrate to provisioned when trailing-30-day serverless compute exceeds the provisioned price at P95 vCores.
options: Auto-pause is broken and cannot be fixed; serverless should be abandoned
Only storage costs prevent pausing; compute always pauses

Keep-awake sources (monitors, pool validation, jobs, tooling) reset the idle clock — each wake-up costs the full delay window; switch back to provisioned when trailing-30-day serverless compute exceeds the provisioned P95 price
Serverless can never be paused; the marketing is false
questions.q: What prevents auto-pause from working, and when should you switch back to provisioned?

title: Azure SQL Serverless: When It Saves vs When It Costs More
